Communities should ensure that residents have access to food safety guidelines and resources, such as emergency food distribution centers or backup refrigeration options. Individuals should be prepared with thermometers to monitor food temperatures and have a plan in place for managing perishable items when power is lost. To extend the life of refrigerated and frozen food, it is important to keep appliance doors closed as much as possible. A refrigerator can typically keep food cold for about four hours, while a full freezer can maintain safe temperatures for up to 48 hours if left unopened. Grouping frozen items can help retain cold temperatures longer. If available, dry ice or frozen gel packs can be used to extend cooling time. The communities can also consider setting up emergency cold storage locations for essential food supplies to assist those without access to adequate refrigeration. If food starts to warm up, strict protocols should be followed to ensure safety. Perishable food should be discarded if it has been above 40°F for more than two hours, as bacteria can grow 43 rapidly at higher temperatures. Any food that smells off, has changed texture, or shows signs of spoilage should not be consumed. Even if it appears fine, items like dairy products, meats, seafood, and cooked leftovers should be thrown out if they have been stored improperly. When in doubt, it is always safer to discard questionable food rather than risk food poisoning. Distribution of thermometers for refrigerators has been previously conducted through Minnesota Power’s Conservation Improvement Program. In addition to individual precautions, community-wide efforts can help mitigate food waste and safety risks during extended power outages. Local organizations, grocery stores, and emergency response teams can work together to distribute non-perishable food and provide food safety information. Residents should also be encouraged to have an emergency supply of shelf-stable foods, such as canned goods, dried fruits, and nuts, to rely on when refrigeration is unavailable. If significant food is lost, the community can work with WLSSD to collect the spoiled food. Information should also be made readily available to community members participating in various food support programs as to the methods of replacing lost food. Water Minimum Resilience Standard: Community members have at least one gallon of water per person per day (CDC), and a clear plan for additional distribution of water has been established. Vulnerability: Everyone is vulnerable to dehydration when there is a lack of drinking water. Those who are most vulnerable include older adults, people with disabilities, children, and low- income individuals or others who may not have the means to store or obtain clean drinking water for emergencies. Additionally, it is important to note that a population’s vulnerability can be dependent on other factors surrounding the outage. For example, everyone is at a higher risk of dehydration during a high heat event.
